top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) rewards a first-order achievement: how technological change and trade shift labour demand, wages and local labour markets. It pairs a framework (skill demand and supply, the education-technology race) with transparent local-labour-market designs. A decade or more of replication and critique has refined the magnitudes and persistence of the China-shock effects but has not overturned the finding of slow, geographically concentrated and costly adjustment. Each named laureate has a distinct, citable role. Katz anchors the skills strand, Hanson the trade-shock evidence, and Autor links the two. The citation should stay on labour demand, wages and local labour markets, claim no priority for the task model and cite no effect sizes. Attribution is the main weakness: Dorn is excluded under the three-name cap, and the two strands could be read as two achievements. If the committee narrowed the scope to import competition, Autor, Dorn and Hanson would be the honest set, but that is not on this slate. P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) is second because of its clean originator attribution and maturity, and it is distinct from the 2022 banking prize. Its quantitative importance is established more indirectly, and it is mainly theoretical. The proposal I ranked first has no marginal-novelty problem as severe as the overlap questions that weigh on the others. Both substantive proposals are preferable to no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for the credited names in P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) or P002 (Kiyotaki, Moore). Disclosed ties: I am a long-time collaborator of Klenow (B017, not on the slate), Aghion and Bergeaud, and my creative-destruction research is adjacent to the 2025 prize themes. I am a frequent co-author of Krusell and a co-author of Hassler, both committee colleagues and IIES colleagues. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
